summary: Describes encodings, identifiers, and parameter formats for using the GOST R 34.10-2012 and GOST R 34.11-2012 algorithms in the Internet X.509 public key infrastructure. It exists to help implementations that want GOST support, and does not imply IETF endorsement of the algorithms. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how certificates can carry the Russian signature and hash tools in the right format.

subtitle: Using Russian cryptographic algorithms in digital certificates.

tldr.problem: Systems need a standard way to use Russian cryptographic algorithms (GOST R 34.10-2012 for signatures and GOST R 34.11-2012 for hashing) in X.509 digital certificates.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines how to encode GOST algorithms, assign them object identifiers (OIDs), specify parameter formats, and include them in certificate structures while maintaining compatibility with the X.509 standard.
tldr.outcome: Certificate authorities and implementations can now interoperably use Russian-approved cryptography in the global PKI, particularly important for organizations in Russia and countries requiring GOST compliance.

today: RFC 9215 is an Informational RFC providing technical specifications for using GOST algorithms in X.509 certificates. It remains the authoritative reference for organizations and implementations that require Russian cryptography in their PKI systems.

sections.title: GOST Algorithms and Digital Certificates
sections.content:
This RFC describes how to use two Russian cryptographic algorithms in the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure. GOST R 34.10-2012 is a digital signature algorithm similar to ECDSA, and GOST R 34.11-2012 is a hash function similar to SHA-2. Both are standardized by Russia's Federal Agency for Technical Regulating and Metrology.

The document specifies the precise encoding formats, object identifiers, and parameters needed to include these algorithms in X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs). It does not imply IETF endorsement of GOST algorithms themselves, but rather provides a technical bridge for organizations that require or prefer Russian cryptography.

Both GOST algorithms come in two variants: 256-bit and 512-bit versions, offering different levels of security. The 256-bit versions produce signatures and hash outputs of 256 bits, while the 512-bit versions produce 512-bit signatures and hashes.
sections.plainLanguage: Russia has its own math-based lock system for signing documents and checking them. This explains how to use those locks in the universal certificate format that the whole world uses.

sections.title: Signature and Hash Algorithm Encoding
sections.content:
The RFC defines unique object identifiers (OIDs) for each algorithm combination. The OID id-tc26-signwithdigest-gost3410-12-256 identifies the 256-bit GOST signature algorithm paired with the 256-bit GOST hash function. Similarly, id-tc26-signwithdigest-gost3410-12-512 identifies the 512-bit versions.

GOST R 34.10-2012 with a 256-bit key produces a signature consisting of two 256-bit integers (r and s), occupying 64 octets total. The 512-bit variant produces a signature of 128 octets. The signature value must be converted from octet string representation to the bit string format used in X.509 certificates and CRLs.

The GOST R 34.11-2012 hash function is similarly identified with separate OIDs for 256-bit and 512-bit variants. When these OIDs appear in an algorithm identifier, the parameters field must be omitted—the algorithm is fully specified by the OID itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Each type of lock gets a unique code number. The 256-bit lock and the 256-bit check are one combination, and the 512-bit versions are another. The signature is stored as a specific number of bytes.

sections.title: Public Key Identifiers and Parameters
sections.content:
GOST public keys are identified by separate OIDs: id-tc26-gost3410-12-256 for 256-bit keys and id-tc26-gost3410-12-512 for 512-bit keys. When these identifiers appear in a certificate's SubjectPublicKeyInfo field, they must be accompanied by parameters specifying which elliptic curve to use.

The parameters are encoded in a SEQUENCE structure called GostR3410-2012-PublicKeyParameters. This SEQUENCE contains a publicKeyParamSet (the curve identifier) and an optional digestParamSet (the hash function to use with this key). For 256-bit keys, the digestParamSet should often be included, specifying which 256-bit hash to pair with the key. For 512-bit keys, the digestParamSet is typically omitted because the matching is implicit.

The RFC also specifies test parameter sets (marked as test-only) that MUST NOT be used outside of testing scenarios. Production certificates must use approved parameter sets such as the TC26 parameter sets or certain legacy CryptoPro parameter sets.

Public keys themselves are stored as octet strings: 64 octets for 256-bit keys (containing x and y coordinates in little-endian format) and 128 octets for 512-bit keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The public key says which curve and hash to use. Some of these choices are only for testing and must not be used for real certificates.

sections.title: Certificate Extensions for Russian Requirements
sections.content:
Russian regulations require additional certificate extensions for qualified certificates. These extensions carry information about the parties involved and the tools used to create the certificate and key pairs.

Distinguished name extensions include the OGRN (main state registration number for organizations), SNILS (individual insurance account number), INN (individual taxpayer number), and INNLE (organization taxpayer number). Each has a corresponding OID defined in the RFC.

The SubjectSignTool extension identifies the token or software used by the certificate owner to generate signatures. This is a UTF-8 string, typically a vendor name and version number. The IssuerSignTool extension is more complex: a SEQUENCE containing the name of the tool used to generate key pairs, the name of the CA's tool, and conformance notices for both.

Certificate policies are expressed as OIDs grouped into security classes (KC1 through KB2, and KA1). These classes reflect security levels defined by Russian cryptographic regulations, allowing verifiers to understand the security guarantees associated with a certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: Russian law requires extra information in certificates: who the company is, what tool was used to sign things, and how strong the security is.

sections.title: Key Usage and Historical Compatibility
sections.content:
When a KeyUsage extension is present in a GOST certificate, it specifies which operations the key may be used for: digital signature, content commitment (non-repudiation), key encryption, data encryption, key agreement, certificate signing, CRL signing, and others. All nine values are permitted for GOST keys.

If a key is used for key agreement, the keyAgreement flag must be set in KeyUsage, and the encipherOnly and decipherOnly flags may optionally be set. However, both encipherOnly and decipherOnly must never be present simultaneously.

Historically, some implementations used the older GostR3410-2001 parameter format with 2012-era keys. To maintain compatibility with these legacy implementations, a system might optionally include a digestParamSet field even when the standard says it should be omitted. The RFC acknowledges this trade-off: strict standards compliance versus backward compatibility with deployed systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Each key can be used for specific jobs: signing, checking, encrypting, or making shared secrets. Some old programs might need extra information even if newer rules do not require it.
